title: Make Time Count 2026
author: Rishad Tobaccowala
source: The Future Does Not Fit In The Containers Of The Past (rishad.substack.com), October 17,
summary: Rishad Tobaccowala offers six ways to make the most of limited time, starting from the idea that success is spending time in ways that bring joy. He urges eliminating frantic multitasking, then focusing through two filters: comparative advantage, which means doing what you do better than most and delegating the rest, and positive outcome, which means a task should earn money, teach something, help someone or feel good. He adds scaling impact through leverage and momentum, including aligning with the underlying trends driving a firm and accepting that culture change takes multi-year persistence. The remaining principles are emotional: do new things so moments are remembered, give time and undivided attention to others, and stay aware of time's passing. The closing section of the post is an unrelated film recommendation.
points: Activity is not productivity; visible busyness mostly signals lost control of time.
Two filters for focus are comparative advantage, which includes delegating to people or agentic collaborators who do a task better, and a requirement that each task yield a clear positive outcome.
Leaders can scale their time through leverage from writing, speaking and technology, and through momentum by aligning with underlying trends.
Culture change and repairing relationships take multi-year persistence, so expecting quick results sets leaders up to quit early.
Giving others undivided attention and mentoring those who cannot repay you is presented as one of the best uses of time.
quotes: Doing more stuff is not the same as achievement. Activity is not productivity. Showing how busy one is does not indicate much other than we have lost control of time.

However, for many of the errands we run and the assignments we take on at work, it is important to ask if we consider outsourcing or delegating to a person or colleague who is better than us in getting that task or expertise delivered.

We should only do things which give us a positive outcome. Either we 1) earn a financial reward, 2) learn something new, 3) help someone else ( sometimes this is a difficult and hard but it creates a positive outcome for another person) or 4) the experience itself feels good.

Similarly when we focus on changing the culture of our firm or correct a relationship it is key to aware of the difficulty, the time and the setbacks we will face and the multi-year persistence that will be needed.
Nothing is as rewarding as helping other people, mentoring younger people, paying attention to those who cannot help or give us much in material or career gain.
Respect other people’s time. A big gift is to give people our undivided attention.
If we think not of the lack of time but the beauty of time, we will find that the time we spend is magical.
